paper_title: HIVE-Bench: Evaluating Patch-Level Visual Representations for Egocentric Robot Manipulation

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Pretrained vision is a common start for robot learning, but most comparisons still score one pooled vector from a third-person image. Bimanual policies instead read dense patch tokens from cameras on the robot. We introduce HIVE-Bench: one shared flow-matching policy reads 20 encoders from seven families on 24 egocentric bimanual tasks, across adaptation, task sharing, and sweeps of data, model size, and layer. Keeping the patches matters. Averaging each view to one token removes most of the success, adaptation helps every pair we test, and one shared policy keeps most of the success of separate policies at a fraction of the updates. The same tokens are then scored with statistics, state and object readouts, published vision scores, and an inverse-dynamics readout. That readout of the commanded motion is one of the strongest measurements available before a policy is trained. Recognition, depth, and correspondence do not transfer reliably. Fine-tuning can improve the action readout even when other measurements move the other way, and no statistic is stable enough to replace a rollout before any deployment.

sections.title: 1 Introduction
sections.content: Robot manipulation policies increasingly reuse pretrained visual encoders instead of learning vision from scratch, which transfers poorly across objects, robots, and viewpoints [15]. The candidates come from very different signals, including self-supervision, language alignment, 3D reconstruction, robot data, and visionlanguage models [610]. Choosing among them still means training and rolling out policy. benchmark with shared policy can reveal which representations transfer, and whether inexpensive measurements explain their successes and failures across different training conditions. Earlier evaluations often read pooled third-person feature and relate scene reconstruction to control [2, 3, 11 15]. Bimanual policies do not use that interface. They attend to dense patch tokens, which keep the local detail that separates nearby grasps [1619], and they see through head and wrist cameras that move with the robot and are often occluded [2023]. We therefore ask how encoders compare when one policy reads their patch tokens from onboard cameras, and which properties of those tokens track the resulting success. We introduce HIVE-Bench (Figure 1), to our knowledge the first comprehensive benchmark of patch-level representations for egocentric bimanual manipulation that jointly studies control and diagnostic correlations across training regimes. flow-matching action head [24, 25] reads 20 encoders from seven families on two egocentric bimanual suites [22, 26]. We train it frozen and fine-tuned, on one task and on shared suite, and we sweep data, model size, and the extracted layer, because ranking from single regime is easy to over-read. The same tokens are then scored in several ways: token statistics, state and object readouts, published vision benchmarks, and an inverse-dynamics readout (IDM) that recovers the commanded motion. Those runs support three simple conclusions. Keeping the patch tokens, rather than averaging each view into one, accounts for most of the success of the encoders we compare this way. Fine-tuning improves every encoder we adapt, and one policy shared across tasks keeps most of the success of separate policies at fraction of the updates. The measurements are the second half of the study. Several of them correlate with success somewhere, but none is stable enough to prove which encoder robot should use. IDM is among the strongest readouts, especially on RoboTwin, yet even its ranking misses the best encoder and fails to predict gains from adaptation. Our goal is to map these relationships and their limits; finding measurements that improve on IDM remains an open research problem. Our contributions are: An egocentric patch-level benchmark: one shared policy reads the dense patch tokens, not pooled vector, of 20 encoders from onboard cameras on two bimanual suites under one shared update budget, through documented token interfaces (Section 3). Evaluation from many angles: single-task and multi-task training, frozen and fine-tuned encoders, demonstration and model-size scaling, extraction layers, pooling, and optional robot state, with the action head and optimizer held fixed (Section 4). study of what tracks success, and where it stops: token statistics, action and state readouts, and published vision scores, compared across suites, task sharing, and adaptation, with the cases where frozen ranking fails to predict improvement kept separate from the cases where it holds, and with IDM among the strongest metrics (Sections 5 and 6).

sections.title: 3 HIVE-Bench
sections.content: HIVE-Bench compares encoders by the closed-loop success of one shared patch-conditioned policy, and asks which measurable properties of the tokens go with that success. The environments that supply the tasks and the policy that reads them are introduced separately below. Appendix gives the implementation and the training recipe.

sections.title: 3.1 Environments and protocols
sections.content: We use 12 RoboCasa-GR1 kitchen tasks, performed by humanoid whose 29-D action adds difficulty [25, 26, 49], and 12 domain-randomized RoboTwin 2.0 tasks, performed by two arms with grippers [22, 50] (Figure 2; Table 23). RoboCasa covers object transfer and cabinet, drawer, and microwave interactions. RoboTwin covers tool use, handover, placement, and articulated objects under randomized clutter, lighting, and textures. The suites differ in robot, action, cameras, tasks, and data at once, so differences between them are observational. Default policies see only the current images. One ablation adds robot state (Section 4.5). 3 Figure 2. Environments. Sample scenes from RoboCasa-GR1 (left), where humanoid with dexterous hands works in varied kitchens, and RoboTwin 2.0 (right), where two arms with grippers work on tabletops with randomized clutter, lighting, and textures. Multi-task training (MT) fits one language-conditioned policy to the twelve tasks of suite. Single-task training (ST) fits separate policy to each RoboCasa task. The closed-loop comparison covers 20 frozen encoders under MT, 17 of them under ST, and five fine-tuned encoders on RoboCasa ST and on RoboTwin MT  (Table 2)  . Further controls vary the number of demonstrations, the checkpoint size, the extraction layer, mean pooling, the state input, and the learned queries of the action head. Every configuration in the main comparison is trained with one seed and evaluated with three evaluation seeds of 50 rollouts per task. suite score is the mean of the twelve task scores, and its deviation propagates the per-task evaluation deviations. three-seed RoboCasa MT study, including its stability analysis, is reported in Appendix C.7.

sections.title: 3.2 Encoders and the token interface
sections.content: The 20 encoders span seven families  (Table 6)  : supervised ViT [51]; the self-supervised MAE, DINOv2, DINOv3, and V-JEPA 2.1 [6, 7, 52, 53]; the geometry-oriented SPA, VGGT-Ω, and LingBot-Vision [9, 54, 55]; the visionlanguage CLIP, SigLIP, SigLIP2, and InternViT [8, 5658]; the robot-oriented VC-1 and Voltron [2, 27]; the multi-teacher Theia, RADIOv2.5, and C-RADIOv4 [14, 28, 29]; and three VLMs, Qwen3-VL and its derivatives DepthVLM and Xiaomi-Robotics-1 [10, 59, 60]. Table 3 lists sizes and token counts. Appendix documents checkpoints and preprocessing. The policy reads every patch token of every view. Class and register tokens are removed, and there is no extra feature normalization at the policy interface. Views are stored at 224 224, giving 196 or 256 tokens per view for patch size 16 or 14. V-JEPA 2.1 resizes to 384 pixels and produces 576 tokens, and each VLM contributes 64 final-layer image tokens. Those VLM states do not depend on the instruction, and we do not use Xiaomi-Robotics-1s action head. Two interfaces mix views before the policy reads them: VGGT-Ω receives RoboTwins three views as one input, and VLMs image tokens of later views can attend to earlier ones. We therefore compare an encoder under documented extraction interface, not in isolation (Appendix B).

sections.title: 3.3 The shared policy
sections.content: The action head is DiT flow-matching model derived from GR00T [24, 25, 61], with 16 blocks of width 768 and twelve heads of dimension 𝑑ℎ = 64 (Figure 3). It operates on 32 learned query tokens and 16 noisy action tokens 𝐻𝑡 . The queries are latent positions for attention, and only the action positions are decoded into velocity. They are distinct from the encoders register tokens, which are discarded before this head sees the image. Eight blocks cross-attend to the context 𝐶𝑡 and eight apply self-attention, in alternation, and adaptive layer normalization conditions every block on the flow time. 𝐶𝑡 concatenates the patch tokens of all views. Multi-task runs append projected features of frozen CLIP text encoder alongside visual tokens for task conditioning, so vision enters the policy only through CrossAttn(𝐻𝑡 , 𝐶𝑡 ) = softmax(cid:0)(𝐻𝑡𝑊𝑄)(𝐶𝑡𝑊𝐾 )/𝑑ℎ(cid:1) 𝐶𝑡𝑊𝑉 . (1) 4 Figure 3. The shared policy. (a) Single-task: patch tokens from frozen or fine-tuned encoder, vision foundation model or VLM, condition DiT action expert that denoises 16-step action chunk. (b) Multi-task: visual and frozen text tokens condition the action expert, with task instructions supplied alongside the visual observations. Flames mark trained modules and snowflakes mark frozen ones. The head regresses the flow-matching velocity toward the normalized 16-step action chunk. The flow time is drawn from Beta(1.5, 1), with eight noise draws per sample, and inference integrates 15 Euler steps on RoboCasa or 10 on RoboTwin. Action heads span 138.669156.478M parameters. Appendix gives complete downstream counts and the flow objective. Each policy is trained for 100k AdamW steps with global batch of 128 on four GPUs, in BF16, with warmup and cosine decay. The budget is equal per policy, not per task, so twelve single-task policies consume twelve times the updates of one multi-task policy on the same suite. The action head uses peak learning rate of 104. Fine-tuning updates the encoder at 105. Other trainable projections use 3 105 on RoboCasa MT and 104 otherwise. Frozen runs update the head and its projections only. Table 3 reports training FLOPs and step time, and Appendix gives the complete recipe.

sections.title: 3.4 Diagnostics and statistics
sections.content: The diagnostics describe each encoder from head-camera frames, before asking which of those descriptions agree with closed-loop success (Appendix E). Token statistics need only frames: patch similarity, norms, covariance rank, spatial frequency, and their change through an episode. Norm-histogram entropy [14] bins each frames patch norms into 30 bins. Features come from the early frames of every fifth demonstration. IDM and state probes use four-layer, width-256 transformers and learned query; only input projections grow with encoder width. The IDM probe reads frames 16 steps apart and predicts the standardized command displacement 𝑎𝑡+15 𝑠𝑡 . single-frame control predicts that same target from 𝐼𝑡 , and the state probe decodes 𝑠𝑡 . An object probe covers four RoboTwin tasks. Because the IDM target contains 𝑠𝑡 , part of it is readable from one frame (Appendix E.2). Published vision scores are collected for the checkpoints that report them under shared protocol, covering classification, segmentation, depth, correspondence, and label propagation (Section 5.2). Associations use Spearmans 𝜌, permutation test, 95% bootstrap interval, and BenjaminiHochberg correction within each cohort. Primary cohorts are the vision encoders; readouts also include the VLMs. Family deletion and paired beforeafter comparisons test whether an association depends on related encoders or on adaptation (Appendix E.3). These measurements are cheaper than training the policy. Token statistics need only demonstration frames, the probes train for four epochs on frozen tokens, and the vision scores come from published evaluations rather than new robot runs. Section 5 then asks which of them agrees with closed-loop success, and which of those agreements disappear when the benchmark or the training regime changes. 5 Figure 4. sections.title: 4 What Makes a Visual Representation Useful for Control?
sections.content: We first examine the policy interface, then encoder choice, task sharing, scale, and additional inputs. Success rates are percentages; changes are in percentage points.

sections.title: 4.1 Preserve spatial tokens, then adapt the encoder
sections.content: Mean pooling discards much of the information the policy uses. Replacing each views patches with their mean and retraining the same head reduces DINOv2 from 32.28% to 9.94% and DINOv3 from 31.22% to 6.44% on RoboCasa MT (Figure 4a). The loss appears in 23 of 24 encodertask pairs (Appendix C.2). Scene identity can survive pooling while local distinctions needed to act disappear; evaluating individual patches exposes that difference. Fine-tuning improves success, with returns that depend on the encoder. Jointly adapting five encoders and the head improves all ten benchmark pairs (Figure 4b): gains span 1.119.44 points on RoboCasa ST and 2.2226.06 on RoboTwin MT. VGGT-Ω rises from 50.00% to 76.06% on RoboTwin, whereas DINOv2 moves from 49.39% to 51.61%. The five retain their frozen ordering there; on RoboCasa, DINOv3 overtakes DINOv2 and VC-1. strong starting point and large return to adaptation are distinct advantages (Appendix C.2).

sections.title: 4.2 Multi-task performance across encoders
sections.content: Strong encoders emerge from several pretraining families. We next hold the patch-conditioned interface fixed and compare the full encoder suite under MT  (Table 3)  . VGGT-Ω leads RoboCasa at 35.39%, followed by C-RADIOv4 at 34.78% and DINOv2 at 32.28%. The three VLMs lead RoboTwin at 51.44 53.67%. Cross-benchmark ranks agree only moderately (𝜌 = 0.43): VC-1 outperforms V-JEPA 2.1 on RoboCasa but trails it on RoboTwin. Pretraining family alone is too broad label to settle the choice; the target setting changes which strengths matter. Cost also changes the choice. DINOv2 comes within 3.11 points of VGGT-Ω on RoboCasa at 54.8 versus 113.3 TFLOPs per step, while the VLMs lead RoboTwin at 195.3 TFLOPs per step. shared optimizer schedule therefore does not make the encoders equally expensive to train, and the cheaper run can be the practical choice when the success gap is only few points.

sections.title: 4.4 More demonstrations help more consistently than more parameters
sections.content: Additional demonstrations improve every curve. We retrain policies on nested demonstration subsets with the same update budget. Increasing demonstrations per task from 50 to 1,000 adds 24.4428.16 7 points across RoboCasa MT encoders. All RoboTwin curves improve from 50 to 500; SigLIP2 gains 34.94 points and overtakes DINOv3 (Figure 5a,b). On matched RoboCasa tasks C1C4, doubling 500 to 1,000 adds 10.3313.00 points for MT, versus 0.17 to +3.83 for ST. Shared policies still benefit where task-specific curves flatten (Appendix C.3). The value of model scale depends on the family. Within-family sweeps show less uniform return. DINOv2 improves from Small to Base, then plateaus on RoboTwin and declines on RoboCasa; DINOv3 Base is its familys strongest RoboCasa checkpoint. V-JEPA 2.1 instead rises from 18.67% to 36.22% on RoboCasa between Base and giant, and reaches 55.89% on RoboTwin. VC-1 Large improves on both suites (Figure 5c,d). Scale helps when the additional capacity transfers to the policy.

sections.title: 4.5 Input and extraction choices have different returns
sections.content: Robot state and finer image grids give smaller gains. Two controls test whether missing proprioception or coarser grid explains the encoder gaps. state token improves DINOv2 and RADIOv2.5 by 0.392.97 points and preserves their ordering (Figure 6a,b). More than doubling DINOv3s tokens, from 196 to 400, adds 1.17 and 4.17 points. Both effects are smaller than retaining patches in the first place, so the image stream, not missing state token, carries most of the gap. An intermediate layer can recover much of VLMs RoboCasa deficit. Replacing final-layer features with layer 16 tests whether useful information is easier to read earlier in the network. Qwen3-VL and Xiaomi gain 811 points on RoboCasa and change by less than point on RoboTwin (Figure 6c). The useful layer is not the same for every model, just as the useful size is not the same for every family (Appendices C.5C.6).

sections.title: 5.1 Action readout is informative, but shares a static component
sections.content: IDM is one of the strongest readouts of closed-loop success. We ask which cheap measurement best ranks frozen encoders before policy is trained. Among vision encoders, two-frame IDM error correlates with RoboTwin MT success at 𝜌 = 0.75 (95% interval [0.90, 0.40], 𝑞 = 0.020), and removing any pretraining family leaves 𝜌 between 0.88 and 0.70. The association keeps the expected sign on the tasks we test. IDM is thus strong correlate on RoboTwin, although even this association does not reliably identify the best encoder for control. Matching probe capacity preserves the state association. With the same width-256 transformer, state error correlates with success at 0.44, 0.39, and 0.62 across the three vision cohorts. Including VLMs leaves associations of 0.53, 0.50, and 0.50  (Table 4)  . Object error behaves differently: its RoboTwin correlation changes from 0.54 to 0.05 with VLMs. Recovering robot configuration and object position therefore give different assessments of the same representations. future frame improves prediction, but does not isolate motion. Because the target includes 𝑠𝑡 , IDM and state errors move together (𝜌 = 0.80 and 0.82). future frame lowers error for every frozen encoder, by 40.7% and 46.9% at the median, but the encoder order barely changes. The second view therefore adds information without changing which encoder looks best. This control tests access to later observation, rather than isolating motion understanding. Figure 7. Different settings favor different diagnostics. (a) Associations with success among vision encoders. Error signs are reversed; other metrics retain their signs. Bold cells have 𝑞 < 0.05 among primary diagnostics. (b) DINOv3 minus DINOv2 at matched sizes: vision gains and control losses point in opposite directions. Differences use each metrics score points. 9 Fine-tuning improves action readout without uniformly improving scene readout. Repeating the readouts after policy learning separates adaptation from cross-encoder differences. All five paired RoboTwin encoders improve success and lower both IDM and state error, yet four increase object error (Figure 8). The gain in success and the gain in object readout are not the same change. Policy learning favors action-relevant information without improving every scene readout. Figure 8. Following encoders through fine-tuning on RoboTwin. Arrows join frozen (open) and adapted (filled) checkpoints. Gray points show frozen defaults; blue diamonds add other model sizes. Action error falls consistently, while object error and temporal entropy need not improve with success. The first two horizontal axes are logarithmic. Pooling adapted checkpoints with frozen encoders strengthens the IDM correlation to 0.80, versus 0.40 within the adapted group. Frozen IDM error does not order adapted success. The pooled relationship mostly separates frozen from adapted representations, so it is weak guide to which encoder to fine-tune. strong correlation across the pooled set can be read as evidence about adaptation when it is only evidence about the frozen starting points. Broad associations also leave room for size and layer reversals. Across size variants the IDMsuccess correlation remains negative, yet DINOv2 Base to giant lowers IDM error while success falls. Qwen and Xiaomi likewise improve both readouts at layer 16 on RoboTwin, with little change in success. Size and layer are changes inside one model, and cross-encoder correlation need not survive them. readout can separate pretrained encoders without predicting every change inside one model.

sections.title: 5.2 Better vision scores do not reliably imply better control
sections.content: Published vision scores provide no consistent ordering for control. Matched checkpoints for classification, segmentation, depth, correspondence, and label propagation [29, 52, 55] show no nominal association with multi-task success on either suite (Appendix E.6). ImageNet linear-probe accuracy gives 𝜌 = 0.07 on RoboCasa and 0.38 on RoboTwin. Matched sizes sharpen the contrast. DINOv3 gains 1.656.37 mIoU on ADE20k and 1.92.9 NAVI points over DINOv2, yet loses 1.068.56 success points on RoboCasa and 18.9422.33 on RoboTwin (Figure 7b). high score on vision benchmark can sit next to strong policy, but the improvement on the benchmark is not the improvement in control.

sections.content: More diagnostics help selectively. Nested family-held-out prediction tests whether diagnostics complement one another  (Table 5)  . The same screen falls below random selection on both RoboCasa regimes  (Table 20)  . shortlist can therefore sit close to the best encoder and still miss it, which is why the remaining candidates are checked with policy runs. The benchmark matters more than task sharing. Profiles agree much more closely within RoboCasa (𝑟 = 0.95) than between the two benchmarks (𝑟 = 0.65), so changing the robot and the views changes which properties accompany success. Sharing the tasks barely changes that profile, and diagnostic chosen on single-task data remains informative when those tasks are trained together.

sections.title: 6 Discussion and Conclusion
sections.content: HIVE-Bench connects dense egocentric representations to the policies that use them. Preserving patches, adding demonstrations, and adapting features improve control, and task sharing broadens coverage cheaply. IDM is one of the strongest guides to which frozen encoder will succeed, but no measurement is stable enough to prove that choice. Three physical tasks preserve DINOv2s lead over DINOv3 and CLIP (Appendix D). The other evidence uses one head and two suites, so more tasks and seeds are still needed. The open question is how to improve on IDM while keeping closed-loop success as the final measure.
